title: Stop Thinking in Yes/No. Start Thinking in Odds.
subtitle: Almost nothing is certain, yet your brain demands a yes or a no. Learning to answer in numbers is the single biggest upgrade to how you think.
hook: "Will it rain tomorrow?" Your brain wants a yes or a no. But the honest answer is a *number* — like 30%. The universe runs on uncertainty, and the people who navigate it best share one habit: they stopped demanding certainty and started thinking in **probabilities**. Master this and you get a superpower — Bayes' theorem, smart bets, and a nose for when your gut is lying to you. Lesson one of Ideas & Minds.

sections.heading: A probability is just a slice
sections.body:
A probability is a number from **0 (no way)** to **1 (dead certain)**, often shown as a %. The cleanest mental image: out of everything that *could* happen, what fraction is the thing you care about?

Roll a fair die: 6 equally likely faces. Rolling a 4 is **1 of 6 ≈ 17%**. Rolling an even number is **3 of 6 = 50%**. That's the whole engine: favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, when each is equally likely. Not scary. Just counting.

sections.caption: Probability = your slice of all the ways things could go. The 'sample space' is everything possible; the event is the part you want.

sections.label: The pro move: say a number
sections.body: Two honest ways to read a probability. **Frequency:** over many tries, how often? (A coin is heads ~50% of many flips.) **Belief:** how sure am I about this one-off? ('70% this launch ships on time.') You can't 'repeat' a launch — but you can still commit to a number. Forcing yourself to say '~60% sure' instead of 'probably' instantly makes you sharper. That belief-view is the seed of Bayes' theorem, coming soon.

sections.heading: The two rules that cover most of life
items: **AND (independent):** multiply. Two coins both heads = ½ × ½ = **¼**.
**OR (mutually exclusive):** add. Rolling a 1 or a 2 = ⅙ + ⅙ = **⅓**.
Everything fancier is built on these two moves plus careful counting.

sections.caption: A clean primer on sample spaces, events, and computing simple odds.

takeaways: A probability is **0 to 1**: favorable ÷ total equally-likely outcomes.
Two readings: long-run **frequency**, and **degree of belief** in a one-off.
Your gut over-trusts high odds and ignores base rates — numbers fix that.
Saying an actual number ('~60%') beats vague words and sets up Bayes next.

Flip a fair coin twice. P(heads BOTH times)?
BOSS: A test is '90% accurate' and you test positive for a super-rare disease. Why might you STILL probably be fine?
options: Because the disease is so rare, most positives are false alarms (base rate)
You can't be fine after a positive
quiz.explain: When something is rare, even an accurate test throws off lots of false positives. Ignoring the base rate is the classic probability trap — and exactly what Bayes fixes.

tg_quiz.q: Flip a fair coin twice — chance of heads both times?
tg_quiz.correct: Nice — AND means multiply: ½ × ½ = ¼.
tg_quiz.wrong: Close — for 'both', multiply: ½ × ½ = ¼.
